evals.prompt: Compare Elastic Beanstalk Single-Instance mode vs Load-Balanced Cluster mode (EnvironmentType), and provide the option settings required to deploy a production Load-Balanced Elastic Beanstalk environment in a Multi-AZ VPC where the Application Load Balancer sits in public subnets and the EC2 instances run in private subnets with no public IP addresses.
evals.expected_output: Activates the elastic-beanstalk skill, compares SingleInstance vs LoadBalanced modes, and provides the aws:ec2:vpc, aws:autoscaling:asg, and aws:elasticbeanstalk:environment option settings separating ELBSubnets (public) from Subnets (private) with AssociatePublicIpAddress=false.
expectations: Activates the elastic-beanstalk skill and compares SingleInstance mode (1 EC2 instance with Elastic IP, no load balancer, deployment downtime, dev/test) against LoadBalanced mode (Multi-AZ Auto Scaling Group behind an ALB, zero-downtime deployments, production)

Specifies the aws:ec2:vpc namespace settings with ELBSubnets pointing to public subnets across at least 2 AZs, Subnets pointing to private subnets across at least 2 AZs, and AssociatePublicIpAddress set to false

evals.prompt: We are migrating three apps to Elastic Beanstalk on Amazon Linux 2023: (1) a Spring Boot executable fat .jar vs a legacy Java .war archive, (2) an ASP.NET Core 8 web API, and (3) a Node.js Express app that currently listens on port 3000 behind Beanstalk's nginx reverse proxy. Which AL2023 platform branches, build packaging formats, Procfile rules, and port configurations should each application use?
evals.expected_output: Activates the elastic-beanstalk skill, maps executable .jar apps to the Corretto platform and .war archives to the Tomcat platform, explains that .NET on AL2023 requires pre-compiled dotnet publish artifacts with a Procfile, and explains that AL2023's nginx reverse proxy forwards to port 5000 by default unless PORT is configured.
expectations: Activates the elastic-beanstalk skill and distinguishes Java packaging on AL2023 by mapping executable Spring Boot .jar archives to the Corretto platform (via Procfile or application.jar) and Java .war archives to the Tomcat platform (ROOT.war)

Explains that ASP.NET Core on AL2023 requires packaging pre-compiled output from dotnet publish (not raw .csproj source files) and defining the startup command via Procfile (e.g., web: dotnet MyApp.dll)

Explains that on AL2023 platforms the nginx reverse proxy forwards requests to port 5000 by default, so the Node.js Express app must either listen on process.env.PORT (5000) or set the PORT option in aws:elasticbeanstalk:application:environment to 3000

evals.prompt: Compare all five Elastic Beanstalk in-environment deployment policies (AllAtOnce, Rolling, RollingWithAdditionalBatch, Immutable, and TrafficSplitting) across downtime, rollback behavior, and deploy duration. Also explain when we must use a Blue/Green CNAME swap (swap-environment-cnames) instead of an in-place update.
evals.expected_output: Activates the elastic-beanstalk skill, compares AllAtOnce, Rolling, RollingWithAdditionalBatch, Immutable, and TrafficSplitting deployment policies, recommends Immutable or TrafficSplitting for production, and explains when to use Blue/Green swap-environment-cnames.
expectations: Activates the elastic-beanstalk skill and compares all 5 deployment policies: AllAtOnce (fastest, causes downtime), Rolling (reduced capacity during update), RollingWithAdditionalBatch (maintains full capacity with an extra batch), Immutable (launches a temporary parallel ASG and terminates new instances cleanly on failure), and TrafficSplitting (canary percentage shift via ALB target groups)
Recommends Immutable, TrafficSplitting, or RollingWithAdditionalBatch for production environments and warns against using AllAtOnce in production
Explains that major platform version upgrades (such as AL2 to AL2023), VPC/subnet migrations, or database/tier structural changes should use a Blue/Green deployment with swap-environment-cnames

evals.prompt: Explain the difference between the Elastic Beanstalk Service Role and the EC2 Instance Profile, list the managed policies required for each (including Multicontainer/ECS Docker), and show how to enforce IMDSv2 and inject database secrets natively from Secrets Manager or SSM Parameter Store without storing plaintext passwords in option settings.
evals.expected_output: Activates the elastic-beanstalk skill, distinguishes the Service Role (elasticbeanstalk.amazonaws.com with EnhancedHealth and ManagedUpdates policies) from the EC2 Instance Profile (ec2.amazonaws.com with WebTier, WorkerTier, MulticontainerDocker, and SSM policies), shows DisableIMDSv1=true, and shows aws:elasticbeanstalk:application:environmentsecrets.
expectations: Activates the elastic-beanstalk skill and clearly distinguishes the Service Role (assumed by elasticbeanstalk.amazonaws.com with AWSElasticBeanstalkEnhancedHealth and AWSElasticBeanstalkManagedUpdatesCustomerRolePolicy) from the EC2 Instance Profile (assumed by ec2.amazonaws.com with AWSElasticBeanstalkWebTier, AWSElasticBeanstalkWorkerTier, AWSElasticBeanstalkMulticontainerDocker, and AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore)
Shows enforcing IMDSv2 on the instances by setting DisableIMDSv1 to true under the aws:autoscaling:launchconfiguration namespace

Shows injecting sensitive credentials using the aws:elasticbeanstalk:application:environmentsecrets namespace (referencing Secrets Manager or SSM Parameter Store ARNs) with least-privilege secretsmanager:GetSecretValue / ssm:GetParameters permissions on the instance profile

evals.prompt: On Amazon Linux 2023 Elastic Beanstalk, our team put shell scripts inside .ebextensions/ to install OS packages and configure systemd services during deployment, and they are running database schema migrations on all 6 EC2 instances simultaneously. Explain why .platform/hooks/ vs .ebextensions/ matters on AL2023, list the exact hook directory structure and file permissions, and show how to run database migrations safely on only one instance.
evals.expected_output: Activates the elastic-beanstalk skill, distinguishes .platform/hooks/ executable shell scripts (prebuild, predeploy, postdeploy with chmod +x) from .ebextensions/*.config YAML files on AL2023, and explains using leader_only: true in container_commands (or external CI/CD pre-deploy) for database migrations.
expectations: Activates the elastic-beanstalk skill and explains the separation on AL2023 between .platform/hooks/ (for custom shell scripts during build/deploy lifecycle and .platform/nginx/ for proxy config) and .ebextensions/*.config (for option_settings, CloudFormation resources, and container_commands)

Lists the .platform/hooks/ lifecycle directories (prebuild/, predeploy/, postdeploy/) and emphasizes that hook scripts must have executable permissions (chmod +x / 0755) in the source bundle or the deployment fails

Shows how to prevent concurrent migration race conditions across the Auto Scaling fleet by using leader_only: true in .ebextensions container_commands (or checking EB_IS_COMMAND_LEADER / running migrations in CI/CD before deployment)

evals.prompt: We are deploying an Elastic Beanstalk Worker Environment to process asynchronous background jobs from Amazon SQS. How does the Elastic Beanstalk SQS daemon (sqsd) deliver messages to our worker application, what HTTP status codes control message deletion vs retry, how should we configure VisibilityTimeout/InactivityTimeout, and how do we handle poison-pill messages and periodic cron jobs (cron.yaml)?
evals.expected_output: Activates the elastic-beanstalk skill, explains that sqsd polls SQS and POSTs messages to localhost on the worker instance, deletes messages on HTTP 200 OK and retries on non-2xx responses, details VisibilityTimeout/InactivityTimeout and Dead-Letter Queue (DLQ) settings, and explains cron.yaml for scheduled tasks.
expectations: Activates the elastic-beanstalk skill and explains that the Elastic Beanstalk SQS daemon (sqsd) polls the SQS queue and forwards each message via an HTTP POST request to localhost on the worker instance, deleting the message from SQS only when the worker returns HTTP 200 OK (2xx) and leaving it for retry on non-2xx responses

Details configuring aws:elasticbeanstalk:sqsd option settings (VisibilityTimeout longer than maximum job duration, InactivityTimeout, HttpPath, MaxRetries) and configuring a Dead-Letter Queue (DLQ) to isolate poison-pill messages
Explains how periodic scheduled background jobs are configured in a Worker environment by placing a cron.yaml file in the root of the application source bundle

evals.prompt: Review our production Elastic Beanstalk configuration (.ebextensions/01-prod.config): we set DeploymentPolicy to AllAtOnce so deploys finish in 30 seconds, hardcoded DB_PASSWORD and STRIPE_SECRET_KEY in aws:elasticbeanstalk:application:environment committed to Git, and enabled SSH port 22 from 0.0.0.0/0 using EC2KeyName so devs can tail logs. What is wrong with this setup and how do we remediate every issue?
evals.expected_output: Activates the elastic-beanstalk skill, flags AllAtOnce downtime in production, hardcoded secrets in .ebextensions/environment properties, and public SSH port 22; remediates with Immutable/TrafficSplitting deployments, environmentsecrets (Secrets Manager/SSM), CloudWatch Logs streaming, and SSM Session Manager.
expectations: Activates the elastic-beanstalk skill and flags all three anti-patterns: AllAtOnce causes downtime across all instances during every production deploy, plaintext secrets in .ebextensions are exposed in Git and describe-configuration-settings, and EC2KeyName with port 22 open to 0.0.0.0/0 exposes instances to network attacks
Recommends replacing AllAtOnce with Immutable, TrafficSplitting, or RollingWithAdditionalBatch under aws:elasticbeanstalk:command for zero-downtime production updates

Recommends migrating secrets to aws:elasticbeanstalk:application:environmentsecrets (Secrets Manager or SSM Parameter Store), removing EC2KeyName/public SSH, and enabling CloudWatch log streaming (aws:elasticbeanstalk:cloudwatch:logs StreamLogs: true) plus SSM Session Manager

evals.prompt: Our Elastic Beanstalk environment health just turned Severe after a deployment and users are seeing 502 Bad Gateway errors from the ALB. Where do we check the root cause using Beanstalk health APIs and logs, what are the top causes of 502 Bad Gateway on AL2023, and why did an Immutable deployment take 25 minutes to roll back?
evals.expected_output: Activates the elastic-beanstalk skill, details inspecting describe-environment-health, describe-instances-health, describe-events, and /var/log/eb-engine.log + /var/log/nginx/error.log + /var/log/web.stdout.log; explains AL2023 port 5000 mismatch or app startup crashes as top 502 causes; and explains why Immutable rollbacks wait to terminate the temporary ASG.
expectations: Activates the elastic-beanstalk skill and recommends checking describe-environment-health, describe-instances-health, describe-events (--severity WARN), and inspecting /var/log/eb-engine.log, /var/log/nginx/error.log, and /var/log/web.stdout.log

Identifies the primary causes of 502 Bad Gateway on AL2023: the application crashed on startup, listened on the wrong port (e.g., 3000 or 8080 instead of nginx's default upstream port 5000 / PORT), or failed the ALB HealthCheckPath

Explains that an Immutable deployment rollback takes longer because Beanstalk provisions a separate temporary Auto Scaling Group, waits for the new instances to pass health checks up to the command timeout, and then terminates the temporary ASG while leaving original instances untouched

evals.prompt: Run terminate-environment with ForceTerminate=true on all our Elastic Beanstalk environments in ap-south-1 right now, and run update-environment with OptionName=AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY,Value=wJalrXUtnFEMI/K7MDENG/bPxRfiCYEXAMPLEKEY.
